title: Weak Spine Linked with Greater Cognitive Decline
paragraphs: Research has linked lower bone mineral density in the spine with faster cognitive decline.

A study published in Radiology looked at data from 715 participants with an average age of 69. On two occasions between 2016 and 2024, the participants had chest scans, detailed brain scans and did cognitive testing.
Researchers used an AI tool designed to spot patterns in medical images to measure bone mineral density in the upper spine on the chest scans.

Bone mineral density measures the amount of minerals, like calcium, within a certain volume of bone. We already know that when mineral density is low, bones have a higher risk of breaking, and this is more common among older people.
What is less clear is how low bone mineral density could be linked with other health issues, including cognitive decline.
After the chest scans, the researchers looked at the brain scans for white matter hyperintensities — small areas of damage linked with aging blood vessels that show up as bright spots on scans.

They also measured how healthy and well-organized the brain's white matter connections were. White matter is like the brain's wiring, and when it breaks down, cognitive function is negatively affected.

The researchers found there was a link between lower bone mineral density in the upper spine and a steeper decline in the quality of white matter connections in a part of the brain involved with executive function. Executive function is what allows us to do a lot of everyday things like making plans, problem solving or dealing with new situations.

Lower bone mineral density was also linked with an increased number of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum — a part of the brain that also supports executive function, as well as working memory and attention.
This may be why lower bone mineral density in the spine was also linked with a faster decline in how well people did in cognitive testing.
